headline: An extended validation code signing certificate is held to the subject its own section requires.
summary: The code signing profile read the extensions and left the subject distinguished name alone, so a certificate naming no organization, no country, or a business category the specification does not define passed it. The `cabf-cs` profile now covers sections 7.1.4.2.2, 7.1.4.2.3 and 7.1.4.2.4. Each of those three sections names the certificates it governs, and none of them names a timestamp certificate, so the subject rows are scoped to the code signing arm and an extended validation certificate answers for the fields its own section adds.

Added: The subject fields both arms share (section 7.1.4.2.2): a `commonName` is required, a `domainComponent` is prohibited, and a subject attribute carrying only the metadata characters the clause names, a full stop, a hyphen and a space, is reported. An empty value states the same absence and is read the same way.

The subject fields a code signing certificate must carry (sections 7.1.4.2.3 and 7.1.4.2.4): an `organizationName`, a `countryName` that is a two-letter code, and at least one of `localityName` and `stateOrProvinceName`, since each of those two is required exactly when the other is absent. Section 7.1.4.2.4 carries the address fields onto an extended validation certificate, so both arms answer for them.

The subject fields an extended validation certificate adds (section 7.1.4.2.4): a `businessCategory` that is one of the four strings the clause names, a `jurisdictionCountryName`, and a `serialNumber`. The clause also bounds the jurisdiction fields against the level the incorporating or registration agency operates at, and requires the state or province at the locality level only where the state or province regulates registration there. A certificate carries neither fact, and a country with a locality and no state is conformant for such an agency, so no row grades the relationship and a valid certificate is not failed for it.

The three reserved policy identifiers are read apart rather than together, so `2.23.140.1.3` selects the extended validation arm and `2.23.140.1.4.1` the ordinary one. The extension rules of section 7.1.2.3 ask the same question of both, and the subject rules do not.
Fixed: Which rules a certificate answers for no longer depends on the order its policies sit in. A certificate asserting two reserved identifiers claims both, and the profile read only the first, so one asserting the ordinary code signing identifier ahead of the extended validation one escaped every extended validation rule while the same certificate with those two reversed did not. Section 7.1.6.4 reports more than one identifier, but only for a certificate issued on or after 15 September 2026, so nothing else caught it. A certificate claiming both kinds is now held to both, and to the tighter of the two validity ceilings.
Changed: A subject attribute is read through one reader shared by every rule that asks for one, flattened across the relative distinguished names, because a distinguished name says the same thing whether it carries one multi-valued element or several single-valued ones.
